A write-ahead log (WAL) is a mechanism used by databases to ensure data consistency and durability in case of a system crash. When a database receives a write request to modify data, it first writes the changes to a log file, known as the write-ahead log, before updating the main data structures, such as the B-tree or hash table. 

This log contains a record of all changes that are pending, including the type of change, the data affected, and any relevant metadata. By writing changes to the log first, the database can guarantee that all changes are persisted to non-volatile storage before they are made visible to other parts of the system. 

In the event of a system crash, the database can recover by replaying the changes recorded in the log, effectively "undoing" any incomplete transactions and restoring the system to a consistent state. This ensures that the database remains consistent and operational after a crash, without losing any data that was pending at the time of the failure.

When the database restarts after a crash, it reads the write-ahead log to determine the last committed transaction that was in progress when the system crashed. The database then applies each of these transactions to the database, in order, to bring the database up to the last committed state. This process is called "recovery."
The database is able to recover from a crash by replaying the transactions from the write-ahead log because the log contains not only the changes made by each transaction, but also any undo information that might be needed in case the transaction was rolled back. If a transaction encountered an error or was rolled back during normal operation, the log entry for that transaction would contain the undo information needed to restore the database to its previous state.
Therefore, the write-ahead log allows a database to recover from a crash by allowing it to replay the transactions that were in progress when the system crashed, and by providing the information needed to undo any transactions that may have been rolled back.
